title: Finance mailbox is acting strange
brief: Kestrel Logistics, Durban. Supplier Brightline says they got a 'new bank details' email from Thandi in Finance.

evidence.title: Rule named "."
lines: → move to RSS Feeds, mark as read

question: You're the responder. What do you do FIRST?
options: Reset Thandi's password and tell her
Revoke her sessions, kill the rule, warn suppliers
why: The attacker holds a stolen session in the cloud mailbox. Cut the session and the rule, then stop the money.
walk: A forwarding rule alert is a classic sign of business email compromise.
Amsterdam a few minutes after Durban, MFA passed by a token: the session was stolen, not the password guessed.
Rule named "." hides replies and leaks every invoice: delete it, or they keep watching.
Suppliers already have fake bank details: warn them today, before they pay.

title: An app is reading the CEO's mail
brief: Kestrel Logistics, Johannesburg. Naledi (CEO) clicked 'Accept' on a 'shared document' prompt yesterday.

evidence.title: Naledi's sign-ins
lines: Her password was never used elsewhere

question: You're the responder. What do you contain FIRST?
options: Disable the app, revoke its consent and sessions
why: The app has its own token; her password isn't involved. Disable, don't delete: a deleted app can be consented again.
walk: Consent phishing: no password stolen, she gave an app the keys.
Mail.ReadWrite plus offline_access lets the app read and send mail even while she's offline.
Clean sign-ins are the tell: resetting her password changes nothing for the app.
It's already reading and drafting: stop the app first, then look at what it took.
